title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation for Pressure cleaning (all heights)
audience: Pressure cleaning operators who set prices or plan monthly revenue, including solo operators.
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of a pressure cleaning round as fixed or variable
Calculate monthly break-even revenue from fixed costs and a variable cost percentage
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instruction.heading: What break-even means for a pressure cleaning round
instruction.body: Break-even revenue is the amount of sales that covers all costs exactly, so profit is zero. Below it the round loses money; above it, each further job adds to profit. It helps you set prices, decide when to add a second unit or crew member, and check whether a new channel can pay for itself. Its answer is only as good as the costs and percentages behind it.

instruction.heading: Split costs into fixed and variable
instruction.body: Fixed costs do not change with the number of jobs in a month. For a pressure cleaning round they include vehicle registration and loan repayments, the trailer or unit's finance, insurance, phone and software subscriptions, and any storage or yard rent. Variable costs move with each job. They include detergent, fuel or power used on a job, hoses and nozzles that wear out, subcontractor fees and the card fee on each payment. Express variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period. ANZ defines the two cost types and warns that costs must be covered to avoid running at a loss. Check the percentage across at least three months before you rely on it.

instruction.heading: The formula
instruction.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage. One minus the variable percentage is the contribution margin, the share of each dollar of sales left to cover fixed costs. Use the percentage as a decimal, so 10 per cent becomes 0.10, and the contribution margin is 0.90.

instruction.heading: Work the calculation in order
instruction.body: Write the inputs first, each with its source and date. Compute the contribution margin. Divide fixed costs by it to get break-even revenue. Divide that by your average job price to get the number of jobs, and round up to whole jobs. The job price in this lesson is a reference point: the lead-generation typical for a standard driveway. It is not a price for your business, so replace it with your own average after discounts before you use the result.

instruction.heading: Reconcile before you use any figure
instruction.body: When two figures disagree, go back to the inputs. Confirm that each fixed cost is a monthly amount, not an annual one. Confirm that the variable percentage is a share of sales, not of cost. Confirm that the output is revenue, not profit. Write down the reconciled figure with its inputs, and drop the others. A figure that cannot be checked should not be used to set a price.

procedure: List every monthly cost of the pressure cleaning round and label each one fixed or variable.
Work out variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period, and check it across at least three months.
Calculate one minus the variable percentage to find the contribution margin.
Divide monthly fixed costs by the contribution margin to get break-even revenue.
Divide break-even revenue by your own average job price to get the number of jobs needed each month.
Compare any other break-even figure with your result, reconcile the inputs, and keep only the reconciled figure.

workedExamples.situation: A one-person pressure cleaning round (hypothetical figures, invented for this lesson) has fixed costs of $1,800 AUD a month, variable costs of 10% of sales and an average job price of $250 AUD. The $250 is a reference point from the lead-generation typical for a standard driveway, not this business's price.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many jobs must the round complete each month to break even, and what should it check before setting prices?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contribution margin is 1 minus 0.10, which is 0.90. Break-even revenue is $1,800 AUD divided by 0.90, which is $2,000 AUD a month. At $250 AUD a job, that is exactly 8 jobs, so no rounding is needed. Each job contributes $225 AUD ($250 AUD multiplied by 0.90) towards fixed costs. Seven jobs bring in $1,750 AUD, which is $250 AUD short of break-even. Before setting prices, check that the 10% includes every job cost, that the $1,800 AUD is a monthly figure, and that $250 AUD is the average price actually charged after discounts.

equipmentAndPpe: Cost list for the last three months, labelled fixed or variable

commonErrors.prevention: Convert every cost to the same period before dividing, and label each input with its period.

commonErrors.error: Using variable cost as a share of cost instead of a share of sales
commonErrors.prevention: Divide variable cost by sales for the same period, and write the denominator beside the percentage.

commonErrors.error: Using a lead-generation typical as the job price
commonErrors.prevention: Replace the reference price with your own average job price after discounts.

qualityStandard: Every break-even figure shows its fixed costs, variable percentage, period and source.
Two figures that disagree are reconciled before either one is used in a plan or a price.
documentationEvidence: Cost list split into fixed and variable, with source and date
Reconciliation note wherever two figures disagree
summary: Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage.
Use one period throughout the calculation.
Recalculate from your own inputs, and replace the reference job price with your own average.

knowledgeChecks.question: Break-even revenue is calculated as:
options: Fixed costs divided by (1 minus the variable cost percentage)
Fixed costs multiplied by the variable cost percentage
Sales minus fixed costs, shown as a percentage of the cost

knowledgeChecks.question: A pressure cleaning round has fixed costs of $1,800 AUD a month and variable costs of 10% of sales. What is the monthly break-even revenue?
Two sources give different break-even figures for the same pressure cleaning round. What is the right response?
options: Use the larger figure to be safe and ignore the smaller figure entirely
Recalculate from your own costs and check each source's inputs before using any figure
Average the two figures together and quote the result to the client today
Use the price list alone and skip the break-even check and rely on the owner's gut feel
